title: Report on Studying at Tulane
paragraphs: I had known about the exchange program since I entered university and was interested in it, but being not particularly good at English to begin with, I could not make up my mind to apply and dragged on until I was a fifth-year student. What spoke to my heart was the words of Dr. 粕谷 at a return-report session.

"It is difficult to dramatically improve your English ability in just a few months of study abroad. But what is important is to take on the challenge of this study abroad, overcome it and grow. The students' faces have all changed after they come back."

The wording may be slightly different, but this was roughly the content. Pushed by those words, I decided to study abroad, which was a big challenge for me, and although I could not make preparations I was satisfied with, I studied at Tulane University in the United States for about two months and returned home safely.

I started with the SICU. In the morning, around 6, before the residents came, we gathered, took histories of and examined the patients in the unit, summarised the information and presented it to the resident. There were discussions and mini-lectures there. After usually having breakfast together, the attending came and we presented again about the patients in the unit. The afternoons were relatively free, and I helped with procedures, read papers, and went to watch the surgery of patients scheduled for admission, sometimes taking part as an assistant. Here, the female student who went around with me was very impressive. When she was in a good mood she cheerfully hummed during the clerkship, but when she got hungry she suddenly became grumpy, an amusing person, but she seemed to me to be very excellent. She did rounds and discussions in the ICU with the residents and attendings, and she spoke up frankly to the senior doctors and seemed to remember quite a lot of the test values, which surprised me very much. In Japan, at least in the clerkships at my university, it is hard to see students voicing opinions to doctors. Whether one speaks up or not may partly depend on cultural differences, but it was impressive that she had that much medical knowledge and firmly grasped the patient's condition. They describe clerkships as "work," and depending on the department they do clerkships even on weekends, which made me realise that they take that much responsibility and do practical things.

The second was a clerkship in the ER. In the week before the clerkship started, an email about the shifts arrived. According to it, "For the clerkship, you must complete five shifts in two weeks (10 days). Each shift is either a daytime shift from 7:00 AM to 7:00 PM or a nighttime shift from 7:00 PM to 7:00 AM." I had never imagined I would work night shifts, so I was very surprised, but I also felt anticipation that it would be an interesting clerkship. It was indeed so, and it was a tense and very fulfilling clerkship. In the clerkship, I first went to a patient who had newly come to the examination room and took the history and examined them. Unlike in the SICU, I was required to take a focused history while thinking about the differential, and if I dawdled the resident would come in and start taking the history, so I hurried through to the examination. I organised the content and presented it to the senior doctor, and we discussed the Assessment and Plan, and some doctors even gave mini-lectures when they had time. By repeating the series of history, examination, presentation, receiving feedback, history, and so on, I felt that I was getting the form down, and sometimes I could make use of what I learned by watching the senior doctors' history-taking and examination.

The last was a clerkship in a department called PM&R (Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation), which was something like a pain clinic. For patients with chronic pain, I asked about the course since their last visit, did neurological examinations if necessary, and helped with prescribing drugs. Sometimes I was also allowed to do joint injections under the guidance of the supervising doctor. The boss of this department was a very funny person and showed various past cases with jokes. Not only this boss, but I felt American senior doctors are very enthusiastic about teaching. They teach history-taking, how to examine patients and how to write charts systematically, and what impressed me especially was that they said to the students something like "Have a sense of professionalism and see patients with responsibility." I had never been taught about the mindset of a doctor, and the residents' words were also full of passion, one of the talks that touched my heart.

To sum up this study abroad, I think it was just as Dr. 粕谷 said. As for English, there were of course parts where I improved, but it was not a dramatic leap, and I feel I still have a long way to go. What matters is to use this study abroad as one opportunity to continue studying English from now on. Rather than that, the influence I received from the words of the local students and supervising doctors and the experience of taking action on my own initiative are the big gains from this study abroad, and I think they will remain as assets in the future.
I would like to thank Dr. 粕谷 and the professors and staff of the International Collaboration Office, who gave me this valuable opportunity, and my classmates who studied together with me.
